A longer queue tells a contact center manager that customers are waiting. But it doesn’t explain whether the cause is a staffing gap or a product update generating questions agents haven’t encountered before.


To investigate, a supervisor might review calls from the busiest hours alongside chat transcripts, survey comments, and CRM records.[Contact center](https://sangoma.com/products/contact-center-as-a-service/) analytics software can bring relevant interaction data together, helping teams identify recurring topics and investigate what is driving a change in demand.


For teams evaluating platforms such as[Sangoma CX](https://sangoma.com/products/contact-center-as-a-service/) , the key questions are which analytics capabilities the software supports, which metrics are included, and what actions managers can take with the findings.


## What Is Contact Center Analytics?


Contact center analytics is the process of collecting and analyzing customer interaction data to identify patterns, understand service performance, and guide improvements.


Data can come from[phone-system](https://sangoma.com/products/communications-platform/) call logs, recordings and transcripts, chat and email conversations, SMS and messaging apps, interactive voice response (IVR) menus, post-interaction surveys, and customer relationship management (CRM) records. The sources available depend on the platform and its integrations.


Each source answers a different question. Queue data shows how long someone waited. A transcript reveals why they called. Their CRM history may show that they already contacted support twice about the same issue.


Connecting those details helps a manager distinguish a slow interaction from a recurring problem that needs attention elsewhere in the business.


### Contact Center Analytics vs. Reporting


Reporting summarizes what happened. Analytics investigates the reasons behind the results and, where forecasting tools are available, estimates what may happen next.


A report might show that average wait times increased by 20% last week. Analysis could reveal that a product launch generated more setup questions, while agents needed extra time to find answers. Managers could then update training and help content alongside reviewing staffing.


Comparison Reporting Analytics

## Types of Contact Center Analytics


Most contact centers use several types of analytics side by side.


### Speech and Voice Analytics


Depending on the product, contact center speech analytics can identify keywords, recurring topics, and phrases such as “cancel my account” or “charged twice.”


Contact center voice analytics can gather data on how people speak, including pace, volume, pauses, and other acoustic signals. Vendors use the terms interchangeably or combine both capabilities, so buyers should check what a feature actually analyzes.


Speech analytics might detect an increase in refund conversations, while voice analysis can flag calls with long silences or raised voices, giving supervisors a starting point for reviewing those interactions.


### Text Analytics


Text analytics groups conversations by topic, identifies recurring requests, and may estimate sentiment.


Hundreds of chat messages might fall into a few common themes, allowing managers to investigate the largest or fastest-growing categories.


Topic grouping also helps identify the language customers use. A help article titled “Account credential recovery” may be harder to find than one using the phrase customers actually type: “reset my password.”


### Multichannel Analytics


Multichannel analytics brings reporting from voice, chat, email, SMS, and messaging apps into a shared environment. Teams can compare demand, response times, resolution, and satisfaction across channels.


Comparisons are useful when they account for the reason for contact. If chat resolves fewer password-reset requests than phone support, the chat workflow may need better instructions.


Comparing overall channel averages can hide differences in complexity. A phone queue handling escalations will naturally look different from a chat queue answering basic delivery questions.


### Customer Analytics


Customer analytics follows the customer’s contact history. Interactions are linked to a customer record, usually through a CRM integration or another consistent identifier. Over time, the record shows the channels a customer uses, recurring issues, previous resolutions, and feedback.


Frequent setup questions among new customers may point to an onboarding problem. Repeated escalations among established accounts may reveal a service issue that deserves closer investigation.


### Self-Service Analytics


Self-service analytics examines IVRs, chatbots,[virtual agents](https://sangoma.com/blog/ai-receptionist-vs-ivr-vs-virtual-agent-for-small-business-calls/) , and knowledge bases. The central question is whether customers can complete their task without needing an agent.


If callers repeatedly press “0” at the same IVR menu or open a chat immediately after reading a help article, self-service analytics can help identify where they encounter difficulties. Teams can then investigate which menu options, articles, or workflows need improvement.


### Historical and Real-Time Analytics


Historical analytics helps managers identify recurring peaks, compare periods, and check whether a process change worked. Real-time analytics shows queue lengths, wait times, and agent availability as they change, helping supervisors decide when to move an appropriately trained agent into a busy queue. Depending on the platform, live sentiment or other alerts may also identify interactions that warrant attention.


### Predictive and Prescriptive Analytics


Contact center predictive analytics uses historical patterns to estimate future outcomes, such as interaction volume or customer churn risk.


Prescriptive analytics recommends an action based on those predictions. A forecast might anticipate a rise in billing questions; a prescriptive tool could recommend additional coverage or a relevant next step for an agent.


## How Analytics Improves Contact Center Performance


Why are customers abandoning calls? Why do queues build up every Monday morning? And why do some agents resolve issues faster than others? Contact center analytics helps managers find the answers in their call data and use them to improve staffing, call routing, and customer service.


### Better Customer Experience Through Proactive Resolutions


When contacts about one product or error message begin to rise, the contact center may notice before other teams. Tracking contact reasons over time helps identify spikes early, while transcripts provide product teams with evidence of the issues customers describe. The stakes are real: in[PwC’s 2025 Customer Experience Survey](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/services/consulting/commercial-excellence/library/2025-customer-experience-survey.html) , 29% of consumers said they stopped using or buying from a brand because of poor customer experience.


### Better Agent Performance and Retention


Handle time alone doesn’t explain why an agent takes longer to resolve a call. Reviewing recordings can provide context. If an agent repeatedly puts billing customers on hold to find information, additional training may help. If the whole team searches for the same refund policy, the knowledge base may need updating. Specific, actionable feedback can improve coaching and support agent engagement and retention.


### Smarter Staffing and Lower Operational Costs


Historical data reveals demand peaks, such as Monday mornings, the days after billing statements go out, and seasonal rushes. Scheduling around those patterns helps balance wait times and staffing costs. Staffing is one of the largest contact center operating expenses, making accurate forecasting and scheduling important. Transfer reports can uncover routing problems, too: if calls repeatedly move between the same queues, the IVR may be sending customers to the wrong place first.


### Stronger Compliance and Lower Risk


Supervisors cannot manually review every interaction. Where supported, speech analytics can flag conversations that may need closer review, such as a potentially missed disclosure. These alerts are starting points, not proof of a violation. Organizations handling payment card details should also use appropriate protections to prevent sensitive authentication data from being recorded or retained, rather than relying on analytics to find it afterward.


### Better Customer Retention and Revenue Opportunities


Repeated contacts about unresolved issues can be an early warning sign of customer dissatisfaction. A repeat-contact report can help teams prioritize follow-up and address problems before they affect retention. Conversation patterns may also reveal opportunities to recommend a more suitable product or plan, once the customer’s original issue has been resolved.


## The Key Contact Center Metrics and KPIs to Measure


A measurement framework should cover customer experience, agent performance, operational capacity, and self-service outcomes. Most teams need a small set of priority KPIs, supported by additional metrics for investigation.


Read related measures together. A falling average handle time may look encouraging until first contact resolution also falls and customers begin calling back.


### Customer Experience Metrics


- **Customer satisfaction score (CSAT):** The percentage of survey respondents who rate an interaction as satisfactory, based on the survey’s chosen scale. Report the number of responses alongside the score.
- **Net Promoter Score (NPS):** The percentage of promoters (9–10) minus the percentage of detractors (0–6). NPS measures the customer’s relationship with the company, so it’s a poor fit for scoring individual agents.
- **Customer effort score (CES):** How easy customers found it to get their issue resolved.
- **First contact resolution (FCR):** The percentage of issues resolved during the first contact without a necessary follow-up. Where possible, check repeat contacts across phone, chat, and email; agree on a consistent measurement window.


Not everyone responds to surveys, so repeat contacts, reopened cases, and escalations help provide context that survey scores alone can miss.


### Agent Performance Metrics


- **Average handle time (AHT):** Talk time, hold time, and after-call work, divided by the number of calls handled. Read it alongside FCR, since a short call that leads to a callback saves no time.
- **After-call work (ACW):** Time spent on notes, disposition codes, and follow-ups after a call. High ACW often points to duplicate data entry.
- **Quality assurance scores:** Scores from an evaluation scorecard covering accuracy, required procedures, communication, and resolution.
- **Occupancy:** The share of available time agents spend handling contacts and wrap-up. Consistently high occupancy leaves agents no time to recover between calls.


### Operational Metrics


- **Interaction volume:** The number of contacts in a given period, broken down by channel, queue, contact reason, and time of day.
- **Abandonment rate:** The percentage of customers who hang up or leave the queue before reaching an agent.
- **Transfer rate:** The percentage of interactions passed to another agent or team.
- **Wait time:** How long customers wait for an agent. Check the longest waits too, since the average can hide them.
- **Service level:** The percentage of calls answered within a target time. The common 80/20 benchmark (80% of calls answered in 20 seconds) is a convention, so set a target that fits your customers.


### Self-Service Metrics


- **Containment rate:** The share of interactions that remain within a self-service channel without transferring to a human agent. Containment does not necessarily mean the customer’s task was resolved, so measure completion and repeat contacts alongside it.
- **Deflection rate:** The share of contacts directed away from an agent toward self-service, according to the organization’s definition. A deflected customer may still need help, so track completion and repeat contacts.


## How AI Is Changing Contact Center Analytics


With transcription, topic analysis, and automated scoring, contact centers can review a much larger share of eligible recorded calls, chats, and emails than manual sampling alone allows. The extent of coverage depends on the platform, licensed features, channels, languages, consent requirements, and data availability. Human review remains important for high-impact decisions.


### Searchable Transcripts and Call Summaries


When[audio is transcribed](https://sangoma.com/blog/how-ai-call-transcription-improve-customer-service/) , supervisors can search conversations for a competitor’s name, a product, or a phrase such as “cancel my account.” Where supported, AI summaries can capture the reason for contact, actions taken, and next steps, reducing manual note-taking and helping the next agent understand the history. Agents should still verify amounts, dates, and promised callbacks.


### Sentiment and Intent Across Thousands of Conversations


Intent detection groups conversations by customer requests, such as cancellations, refunds, or upgrades. Sentiment analysis may help supervisors spot changes in the tone of those conversations before enough survey responses arrive to shift CSAT. These scores are imperfect, so check whether the platform analyzes sentiment during a call or only afterward, and how supervisors can validate the results.


### Automated QA Across Eligible Interactions


Automated quality assurance (QA) can evaluate eligible interactions against predefined criteria, such as required disclosures, verification steps, and service quality. The criteria and supported channels vary by product. Supervisors can use the results to prioritize coaching and investigate exceptions, rather than treating automated scores as a substitute for human judgment.


## Contact Center Analytics Mistakes to Avoid


### Tracking Too Many Metrics


When a dashboard shows 40 numbers at the same size, the team ends up chasing whichever one moved this morning. Start with the outcome you want. If the goal is fewer repeat contacts, watch FCR, the top repeat-contact reasons, and customer effort, and keep handle time in the background. Add a metric only when someone has a question it answers.


### Siloed Channels and Data


A customer chats about a billing error, calls two days later, then sends an email. If those contacts sit in separate systems, each may appear resolved even though the customer’s problem remains. Linking phone, chat, and email records to a common customer history makes repeat issues easier to recognize. In a vendor demo, ask to see a chat followed by a call in one customer record.


### Metrics Without Owners or Action


Abandonment spikes, someone mentions it in the weekly meeting, and the same spike is back on the slide the following week. Each priority KPI needs one named owner and a threshold that triggers action. When abandonment crosses that line, the owner checks staffing and routing for that window, makes a change, and reports back on whether it worked.


### Treating AI Scores as the Whole Picture


AI scoring can misinterpret sarcasm, accents, product names, or an agent’s decision to go off-script to solve a problem. If agents cannot challenge inaccurate feedback, coaching loses credibility. Use automated scores to prioritize human review, compare them with manual evaluations, and give agents a way to add context before scores influence performance assessments.


## How to Choose Contact Center Analytics Software


Every vendor demo looks smooth on the vendor’s own data. Ask each one to work through your scenarios with sample reports or call types from your team, so the comparison is fair.


### All Channels in One View


The software should report on the channels your customers use, including voice, chat, email, SMS, and supported messaging apps, without requiring teams to manually combine exports. Ask how the platform links a customer who starts as an anonymous chat visitor and later calls in.


### Built-In Call Recording and Speech Analytics


Confirm whether the platform supports automatic, selective, or manual call recording based on your business and compliance requirements. Check whether transcripts link back to the audio, which languages are supported, who can access recordings, and how long they are retained. Recording and consent requirements vary by jurisdiction.


### Detailed, Customizable Reports and Alerts


Supervisors need live queue views and threshold alerts, while leadership needs trends by team and queue, so role-based dashboards save everyone time. In the demo, ask the vendor to take a high wait-time figure and trace it to the queue and time interval that caused it.


### AI-Powered Quality Management and Coaching


Look for the quality management features your supervisors need, such as automated scoring, call review, live monitoring, and whisper coaching. Whisper coaching lets a supervisor guide an agent during a call without the customer hearing. Ask the vendor to demonstrate how scorecards are configured, how agents see feedback, and how disputed scores are reviewed. Verify which features are native, optional, or delivered through integrations.


### Forecasting and Predictive Tools


Forecasting pays off for larger or fast-growing teams with uneven demand. Check that forecasts cover all your channels and account for handle time, service-level targets, and time agents spend off the phones. A small team with steady volume can usually plan from historical reports and skip the extra cost.


### CRM and Third-Party Integrations


Ask whether the contact center analytics software connects to your CRM out of the box and which data moves in each direction. In the demo, a call should land on the right customer record with its notes and outcome attached. IT teams should also check API access, data export, and who maintains the integration after updates.


### Security and Compliance


Recordings and transcripts may contain personal, medical, or payment information, so check encryption, access controls, retention settings, and audit logs. Ask whether data is processed by third-party AI services and what contractual protections apply. For[healthcare services](https://sangoma.com/solutions/healthcare/) involving protected health information, confirm whether the vendor is acting as a HIPAA business associate, whether a[business associate agreement (BAA)](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html) is required, and which services, recordings, transcripts, and integrations it covers.


### Ease of Use and Scalability


Have supervisors try three everyday tasks: finding a recording, investigating a queue spike, and preparing a coaching review. If these tasks are difficult without vendor assistance, adoption may suffer. Ask about implementation time and training. For pricing, model your call volume and seasonal peaks, including licenses, transcription, AI summaries, storage, and integrations. Check how the price changes as you add agents or channels.

## Contact Center Analytics FAQs


### What is the difference between contact center analytics and reporting?


Reporting shows what happened, such as wait times, call volumes, and service levels. Analytics investigates patterns and possible causes, helping managers decide what to improve. Predictive tools may also estimate future demand.


### What are the most important contact center KPIs to track?


Start with metrics that reflect your goals. Common choices include first contact resolution (FCR), customer satisfaction (CSAT), abandonment rate, service level, average handle time (AHT), and repeat-contact volume. Review related metrics together so that improving one does not create problems elsewhere.


### Do I need AI to analyze contact center performance?


No. Historical reports, queue dashboards, surveys, and manually reviewed recordings can reveal valuable issues. AI can help teams search, classify, and evaluate more eligible interactions, but it is not a prerequisite for effective analytics.


### How can contact center analytics improve customer satisfaction?


Analytics can reveal repeated issues, long waits, unnecessary transfers, and channels where customers struggle to complete tasks. Teams can use those findings to adjust routing, improve knowledge content, coach agents, and measure whether the changes help.


### What should I look for when choosing contact center analytics software?


Prioritize the channels and KPIs your business uses, usable dashboards, access to recordings, customizable reports, supported CRM integrations, security controls, and the ability to test real workflows in a demo. Confirm which AI tools are included and which require add-ons or third-party fees.
